2.text: tribes and nations intermingle.” Raˊlɵ g̣eneˊʟ̣eet (“blended together”) is the

3.text: ordinary Chukchee term to describe intertribal relations on all borders. On the

4.text: other hand, when in 1895, during a brawl at the Anui fair, a Reindeer Chukchee

5.text: was killed by the Cossacks, the others resented the deed so much that they were

6.text: almost ready to attack the fort. Notwithstanding the “weregild” paid by the

7.text: officials to the family of the slain man, the Chukchee harbored a feeling of ill will

8.text: for a long time afterwards; and the next winter, when travelling among the

9.text: Anui camps, I had one or two rather unpleasant encounters with the people.

10.text: A considerable part of their former intractability remains at the present

11.text: time, especially among the Reindeer people, and shows itself even in the minor

12.text: details of every-day life. The Chukchee is easily angered; often a trifle will

13.text: suffice to transform his merry laughter into the most unreasonable rage. They

14.text: themselves are not unconscious of this peculiar feature of their mind. “I am

15.text: a tundra wanderer,” one of my Chukchee acquaintances, named Ñĭroˊn, would
15.note: most consilient explanation is lowercase i with half-abraded breve

16.text: say to me. “My anger rises suddenly. It comes and goes of its own accord.”

17.text: Some women bear a special name on account of their violent temper. They

18.text: are called “quarrelling women” (maraˊ-ñaˊus˙qattê). These are regarded as

19.text: nuisances even by their housemates. Among the men, some have the very

20.text: suggestive epithet “hasty” (qɪvr) prefixed to their names, as “Hasty Aᵋmuˊlin”

22.text: The Chukchee, when angry, growls, shows his teeth, and makes a threatening

23.text: bite on his sleeve or on the handle of his knife, in defiance of his foe. Some

24.text: of them, when angered, shed tears of rage, and tear their hair like unruly children.

25.text: Their language is singularly poor in abusive terms, and quarrels are

26.text: immediately settled by blows or wrestling. There is no lack of murders, some

27.text: of them of a barbarous character. Thus, in a camp near Cape Erri, the son

28.text: and the nephew of the rich reindeer-breeder Yekuˊtku, being goaded to the

29.text: extreme by constant blows and abuse, cut his throat, and that with the knowl-

30.text: edge of his wife, the mother of one of the murderers. In the summer of

31.text: 1896 on the Poplar River, an affluent of the Small Anui, a young man killed

32.text: his brother in order to get possession of his flock. The murderer, with his

33.text: accomplice and their victim, arranged a contest of jumping over a barrier,

34.text: the loser to pay the forfeit of skipping about for a while with his feet and

35.text: hands bound together. When the elder brother lost, the other two men

36.text: accordingly tied his feet, and coolly stabbed him with their knives. I heard

37.text: the details of both deeds from the murderers themselves.

38.text: In the tale of “Elendi and his Sons,” published in my “Chukchee Materials,”

39.text: Elendi, to avenge the treachery of his slave, kills him in a most cruel manner.

40.text: With sharp stakes he fastens the slave’s hands, feet, the fleshy parts of his

41.text: sides, and the skin of his scalp, to the ground, and then makes both of his

42.text: wives urinate and defecate into his mouth.¹
